Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,

spaces ([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $\pi$ be a probability measure on
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$, and let $(P_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$ be a jointly
measurable family of probability kernels on $\mathsf X$: for every
$A\in\mathcal X$, $(\gamma,x)\mapsto P_\gamma(x,A)$ is
$\mathcal G\otimes\mathcal X$-measurable and each $P_\gamma$ is a probability
kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]). Assume that $\pi$ is
invariant for every fixed kernel, meaning $\pi P_\gamma=\pi$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]).

An **adaptive MCMC process** is a pair of measurable processes
$(X_n,\Gamma_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $X_n\in\mathsf X$, $\Gamma_n\in\Gamma$, and
natural filtration $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\Gamma_0,\ldots,X_n,\Gamma_n)$,
such that for every $A\in\mathcal X$,
$$\mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=P_{\Gamma_n}(X_n,A)\quad\text{a.s.}$$
The update rule for $\Gamma_{n+1}$ may depend on the history through time
$n+1$; it is required only to make $\Gamma_{n+1}$ a measurable random variable.

For $n\ge0$, define the adaptation size
$$D_n:=\sup_{x\in\mathsf X}\lVert P_{\Gamma_{n+1}}(x,\cdot)-P_{\Gamma_n}(x,\cdot)\rVert_{\rm TV},$$
where total variation uses the convention
$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal X}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]). Assume each $D_n$
is measurable; it lies in $[0,1]$. The process has **diminishing
adaptation** if $D_n\to0$ in probability as $n\to\infty$. This condition does
not require $\Gamma_n$ to converge.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For a probability kernel $P$ on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), a measurable set $C$ is **$(m,\epsilon,\nu)$-small** if $m\ge1$ is an integer, $0<\epsilon\le1$, $\nu$ is a probability measure ([[def-probability-measure]]), and
$$P^m(x,A)\ge\epsilon\nu(A)\quad(x\in C,\ A\in\mathcal X).$$
The inequality is pointwise in $x$ and holds for every measurable $A$.

A **geometric drift inequality outside $C$** consists of a finite-valued measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,\infty)$, constants $0<\lambda<1$ and $0\le b<\infty$, and
$$PV(x):=\int V(y)P(x,dy)\le\lambda V(x)+b\,1_C(x)\quad(x\in\mathsf X).$$
The terms small set and drift are separate hypotheses; neither definition asserts the existence of the other.

When an invariant probability $\pi$ is specified ([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), an **extended geometric drift certificate finite $\pi$-almost everywhere** allows measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,+\infty]$ with $\pi(V<\infty)=1$ and the same pointwise inequality, interpreted in the nonnegative extended reals. This is a separate convention from the finite-valued drift function above. The geometric theorem treats this certificate on $E=\{V<\infty\}$; the original finite-valued convention gives the corresponding bound on the whole state space.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$

mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

We record the finite-horizon construction used below. If $T$ is a
probability kernel on $(S,\Sigma)$, start with any probability measure $\mu_0$
on $S$ (in particular $\mu_0=\delta_s$ for a fixed start $s$). Given a
probability measure $\mu_m$ on $S^{m+1}$, the map
$$\widehat T_m((s_0,\ldots,s_m),A):=T(s_m,A)$$
is a probability kernel from $S^{m+1}$ to $S$, since the last-coordinate
projection is measurable. For $E\in\Sigma^{\otimes(m+2)}$, set
$$\mu_{m+1}(E):=\int_{S^{m+1}}\int_S1_E((s_0,\ldots,s_m),z)\,T(s_m,dz)\,\mu_m(d(s_0,\ldots,s_m)).$$
The inner integral is measurable by [F6]. Sections of product-measurable
sets are measurable, and countable additivity of the rows of $T$ together
with [F7] gives countable additivity of $\mu_{m+1}$; its total mass is one.
For every measurable prefix set $A\subseteq S^{m+1}$ and $B\in\Sigma$,
$$\mu_{m+1}(A\times B)=\int_A T(s_m,B)\,\mu_m(d(s_0,\ldots,s_m)).$$
Thus this recursion gives a probability law for each finite path, with the
stated one-step transition identity; the identity for all prefix events is
the displayed formula for arbitrary product-measurable $A$. Kernel
integration of a nonnegative measurable test $g$ has the corresponding form
$$\int_{A\times S}g(z)\,\mu_{m+1}(d(w,z))=\int_A\int_Sg(z)T(s_m,dz)\,\mu_m(dw),$$
first for simple $g$ and then by [F7]. These identities are exactly the
finite-horizon conditional transition and expectation rules used below.
Kernel compositions used below are kernels as well: iterating
$(K_1K_2)(x,A)=\int K_2(y,A)K_1(x,dy)$ preserves measurable evaluations by
[F6] and countable additivity by [F7]. This applies to probability kernels
and finite subprobability kernels.

Fix any $\gamma$. For $r\ge1$, set $V_r=V\wedge r$. By [F2], $\int(P_\gamma V_r-V_r)\,d\pi=0$. On $C$ the integrand is at most $\lambda v+b$; on $C^c\cap\{V\le r\}$ it is at most $-(1-\lambda)V$; and on $C^c\cap\{V>r\}$ it is at most zero, because $P_\gamma V_r\le\min(P_\gamma V,r)$. Hence $(1-\lambda)\int_{C^c\cap\{V\le r\}}V\,d\pi\le(\lambda v+b)\pi(C)\le\lambda v+b.$ Letting $r\to\infty$ by [F7] gives the uniform finite bound $\pi V\le v+(\lambda v+b)/(1-\lambda)=:K_\pi$.

Put $\lambda'=(1+\lambda)/2$ and $c=b/(1-\lambda')$. Choose $d\ge v$ so $2c/(d+1)<1/4$, then choose $N\ge1$ with $d(\lambda')^N\le1/2$, and finally choose $L>N+1$ with $(\lambda')^L<1/4$. Let $D=\{x:V(x)\le d\}$. For fixed $\gamma$, the killed subprobability kernel $K_\gamma(x,A)=1_{C^c}(x)P_\gamma(x,A)$ satisfies $K_\gamma V\le\lambda'V$. To make its finite paths explicit, adjoin a cemetery point $\dagger$ and equip $\bar{\mathsf X}=\mathsf X\sqcup\{\dagger\}$ with $\bar{\mathcal X}=\{A,A\cup\{\dagger\}:A\in\mathcal X\}$. Define the probability kernel $\bar K_\gamma$ on this measurable space by $\bar K_\gamma(x,A)=K_\gamma(x,A\cap\mathsf X)+1_C(x)1_{\{\dagger\in A\}}$ for $x\in\mathsf X$, and $\bar K_\gamma(\dagger,A)=1_{\{\dagger\in A\}}$. This is measurable: the first term is a kernel evaluation, the second is measurable, and each row has mass one. Step 0.1 constructs its finite path laws. Let $\bar V=V$ on $\mathsf X$ and $\bar V(\dagger)=0$; then $\bar V$ is $\bar{\mathcal X}$-measurable, $\bar K_\gamma\bar V=K_\gamma V$ on $\mathsf X$, $\bar K_\gamma\bar V(\dagger)=0$, and by iteration $\bar K_\gamma^{N+1}\bar V(x)=K_\gamma^{N+1}V(x)$. The event that the killed path is in $\mathsf X$ after $N+1$ transitions has probability $K_\gamma^{N+1}1(x)$. Under the finite $P_\gamma$-path law from step 0.1, the same recursive formula inserts $1_{C^c}$ at each current state, so for $\tau_C=\inf\{m\ge0:X_m\in C\}$ one has $\mathbb P_x(\tau_C>N)=K_\gamma^{N+1}1(x)$.
$$\mathbb P_x(\tau_C>N)=K_\gamma^{N+1}1(x)\le K_\gamma^{N+1}V(x)\le(\lambda')^{N+1}V(x)\le1/2$$
for every $x\in D$. Hence $\mathbb P_x(\tau_C\le N)\ge1/2$.

Iterating $P_\gamma V\le\lambda V+b1_C\le\lambda'V+b$ gives $Q_\gamma V\le(\lambda')^L V+c$. Put $h(x,y)=(V(x)+V(y))/2$. Outside $D\times D$, at least one coordinate has $V>d$ and the other has $V\ge1$, so $(Q_\gamma\otimes Q_\gamma)h(x,y)\le(\lambda')^Lh(x,y)+c\le a h(x,y),\qquad a:=(\lambda')^L+\frac{2c}{d+1}<1.$ This $a$ is independent of $\gamma$.

For $x\in D$, $Q_\gamma V(x)\le d+c$. The residual probability $R_{\gamma,x}=(Q_\gamma(x,\cdot)-\epsilon\nu_\gamma)/(1-\epsilon)$ is well-defined by step 2.1 and satisfies $R_{\gamma,x}V\le(d+c)/(1-\epsilon)$. Consequently $R_{\gamma,x}\otimes R_{\gamma,y}(h)\le H:=(d+c)/(1-\epsilon)$ for $x,y\in D$. All constants here are independent of $\gamma$.

Let $T=\inf\{m\ge1:B_m=1\}$ and let $N_k$ count failed split attempts in the first $k$ transitions. Choose $B\ge\max\{1,(1-\epsilon)H/a\}$ and define $Z_k=a^{-k}B^{-N_k}h(X_k,Y_k)1_{\{T>k\}}.$ For each finite horizon, the coordinate process under its path law from step 0.1 is a nonnegative supermartingale with respect to its coordinate filtration: on $\{T>k\}$ an outside-$D\times D$ update contracts expected $h$ by step 2.2 and leaves the flag and failure count unchanged; on $D\times D$ a successful split makes the indicator zero, while the failed-split contribution has ratio at most $(1-\epsilon)H/(aB h(X_k,Y_k))\le1$ because $h\ge1$. Since $T\ge1$, $Z_0=h(x,y)$, and therefore $\mathbb E_{x,y} Z_k\le h(x,y)$ for every finite $k$.

For every integer $j\ge1$, the probability of at least $j$ failed split attempts is at most $(1-\epsilon)^j$, by conditioning successively at the first $j$ attempts. On $\{T>k,N_k<j\}$, $Z_k\ge a^{-k}B^{-(j-1)}$, so Markov's inequality [F8] gives $\mathbb P_{x,y}(T>k)\le(1-\epsilon)^j+a^kB^{j-1}h(x,y).$ Choose $\theta>0$ with $aB^\theta<1$ and take $j=\max(1,\lfloor\theta k\rfloor)$. $A\in\mathcal X$, $(\gamma,x)\mapsto P_\gamma(x,A)$ is
$\mathcal G\otimes\mathcal X$-measurable and each $P_\gamma$ is a probability
kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]). Assume that $\pi$ is
invariant for every fixed kernel, meaning $\pi P_\gamma=\pi$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]).

An **adaptive MCMC process** is a pair of measurable processes
$(X_n,\Gamma_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $X_n\in\mathsf X$, $\Gamma_n\in\Gamma$, and
natural filtration $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\Gamma_0,\ldots,X_n,\Gamma_n)$,
such that for every $A\in\mathcal X$,
$$\mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=P_{\Gamma_n}(X_n,A)\quad\text{a.s.}$$
The update rule for $\Gamma_{n+1}$ may depend on the history through time
$n+1$; it is required only to make $\Gamma_{n+1}$ a measurable random variable.

For $n\ge0$, define the adaptation size
$$D_n:=\sup_{x\in\mathsf X}\lVert P_{\Gamma_{n+1}}(x,\cdot)-P_{\Gamma_n}(x,\cdot)\rVert_{\rm TV},$$
where total variation uses the convention
$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal X}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]). Assume each $D_n$
is measurable; it lies in $[0,1]$. The process has **diminishing
adaptation** if $D_n\to0$ in probability as $n\to\infty$. This condition does
not require $\Gamma_n$ to converge.

Use the adaptive MCMC setup of [[def-diminishing-adaptation]]. For
$\epsilon>0$, a state $x\in\mathsf X$, and a fixed parameter $\gamma\in\Gamma$,
define the convergence time
$$M_\epsilon(x,\gamma):=\inf\{m\in\mathbb N:m\ge1,\ \lVert P_\gamma^m(x,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\epsilon\},$$
with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$. The power $P_\gamma^m$ is the $m$-fold
composition of the fixed kernel $P_\gamma$; it is not the adaptive transition
law. Assume $M_\epsilon(X_n,\Gamma_n)$ is measurable for each $n$ and
$\epsilon>0$.

For a specified initial probability law $\mu_0$ of $(X_0,\Gamma_0)$, the
adaptive process has **containment** if for every $\epsilon,\delta>0$ there is
an integer $N=N(\epsilon,\delta)$ such that
$$\mathbb P_{\mu_0}\!\left(M_\epsilon(X_n,\Gamma_n)\le N\right)\ge1-\delta\quad\text{for every }n\ge0.$$
A fixed initial pair $(x_*,\gamma_*)$ is the special case
$\mu_0=\delta_{(x_*,\gamma_*)}$, equivalently the same probability bound
conditional on $X_0=x_*$ and $\Gamma_0=\gamma_*$. Thus containment says that
the fixed-kernel convergence times, evaluated at the current state and
parameter, form a sequence bounded in probability under the specified initial
law. It does not assert a uniform deterministic bound for every possible
state and parameter.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $(X_n,\Gamma_n)$ be an adaptive MCMC process with adaptation sizes $D_n$
as in [[def-diminishing-adaptation]]. For integers $n\ge0$ and $N\ge1$, define
the frozen-kernel mixture $Q_{n,N}$ by
$$Q_{n,N}(A):=\mathbb E\!\left[P_{\Gamma_n}^{N}(X_n,A)\right]\quad(A\in\mathcal X).$$
Then $Q_{n,N}$ is a probability measure and
$$\left\lVert\mathcal L(X_{n+N})-Q_{n,N}\right\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}\mathbb E[D_{n+j}],$$
where the inner sum is $0$ for $i=0$.

Assume simultaneous uniform ergodicity and fix a desired tolerance $\eta>0$. Choose $N=N(\eta/2)$ as in alternative 1. For the frozen mixture $Q_{n,N}$ from [F6], every state and parameter has $\lVert P_{\Gamma_n}^{N}(X_n,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\eta/2$, so convexity of the setwise supremum gives $\lVert Q_{n,N}-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\eta/2$.

On the event $M_\epsilon(X_n,\Gamma_n)\le N$, the definition gives an iterate $m\le N$ within $\epsilon$ of $\pi$; [F5] propagates this bound to the $N$th iterate. On the complementary event total variation is at most one. Therefore the frozen mixture satisfies $\lVert Q_{n,N}-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\epsilon+\delta=2\eta/3$ for every $n$.

The triangle inequality and step 1.2 yield $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\lVert\mathcal L(X_{n+N})-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\eta/2$. As $n+N$ ranges over all sufficiently large times and $\eta>0$ is arbitrary, the asserted convergence follows in alternative 1.

The same fixed-block bound [F6] tends to zero by step 1.1. The triangle inequality gives $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\lVert\mathcal L(X_{n+N})-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le2\eta/3<\eta$. Again $N$ is fixed and $\eta$ is arbitrary, proving the asserted convergence in alternative 2.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. $$\mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=P_{\Gamma_n}(X_n,A)\quad\text{a.s.}$$

$n+1$; it is required only to make $\Gamma_{n+1}$ a measurable random variable.

$$D_n:=\sup_{x\in\mathsf X}\lVert P_{\Gamma_{n+1}}(x,\cdot)-P_{\Gamma_n}(x,\cdot)\rVert_{\rm TV},$$

  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$

  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$

$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

derivations.claim: Every displayed matrix has probability rows, is symmetric, and has column sums one. Thus each is a probability kernel and $\pi P_i=\pi$ by [F1] and [F3]. For a two-state symmetric kernel with flip probability $q$, $(\delta_x-\pi)P=(1-2q)(\delta_x-\pi)$; induction gives $P^m(x,\cdot)-\pi=(1-2q)^m(\delta_x-\pi)$. For $P_0$ and $P_1$, $|1-2q|=4/5$, while $P_2=\Pi$ reaches $\pi$ in one step. Since $\lVert\delta_x-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}=1/2$ by [F4], $$\sup_{x\in\mathsf X,\,i\in\{0,1,2\}}\lVert P_i^m(x,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\tfrac12(4/5)^m\quad(m\ge0).$$ The family is simultaneously uniformly ergodic.

For $k\in\mathbb N$, let $L_k=2^{2^k}$ and $s_k=\sum_{j<k}L_j$, the number of transitions before block $k$. Since $\sum_{j<k}L_j\le k2^{2^{k-1}}$, $$\frac{s_k}{L_k}\le k2^{-2^{k-1}}\longrightarrow0.$$

For each $k$, equip the finite space $$\Omega_k=\{0,\ldots,k\}\times\{1,\ldots,10\}^{L_k}$$ with its uniform probability measure. Write a coordinate as $(J_k,U_{k,0},\ldots,U_{k,L_k-1})$ and put $I_k=1_{\{J_k=0\}}$. Direct counting gives $\mathbb P(I_k=1)=1/(k+1)$; conditional on any value of $J_k$, the $U_{k,t}$ are independent and uniform on $\{1,\ldots,10\}$, with a law not depending on $J_k$. The countable product over $k\in\mathbb N$ exists by [F6] under [A1]–[A2].

In block $k$, for its first transition $n=s_k$ set $\Gamma_n=2$ and use $U_{k,0}$ to draw from $P_2$ (the next state is $0$ iff $U_{k,0}\le5$). For $n=s_k+t$ with $1\le t<L_k$, set $\Gamma_n=2$ if $I_k=0$; if $I_k=1$, set $\Gamma_n=0$ when $X_n=0$ and $\Gamma_n=1$ when $X_n=1$. Use $U_{k,t}$ to sample the selected matrix row: for $P_0$ use thresholds $9$ and $1$ for rows $0$ and $1$ respectively, for $P_1$ use thresholds $1$ and $9$, and for $P_2$ use threshold $5$; the next state is $0$ exactly when $U_{k,t}$ is at most the row's threshold. This recursively defines measurable $X_n$ and $\Gamma_n$. Each next $U_{k,t}$ is independent of the gate and earlier block coordinates by [F2] and the finite product counting in step 1.3; different blocks have the product marginals in [F6]. Therefore conditional on the history, $X_{n+1}$ has law $P_{\Gamma_n}(X_n,\cdot)$, so this is an adaptive MCMC process with the stated kernel family.

If $I_k=0$, every parameter in block $k$ is $2$, and the next block also starts with parameter $2$; hence $D_n=0$ at every transition whose current block has gate zero. If $I_k=1$, then $D_n\le1$. For each $n$ in block $k$, $$\mathbb P(D_n>0)\le\mathbb P(I_k=1)=1/(k+1)\longrightarrow0$$ as $n\to\infty$, because each block is finite and its index tends to infinity. Thus $D_n\to0$ in probability by [F5].

Conditional on $I_k=1$, for each $1\le t<L_k$ the active rule uses $P_0$ from state $0$ and $P_1$ from state $1$. In either case the next state is $0$ iff $U_{k,t}\le9$. Hence $$Z_{k,t}:=1_{\{X_{s_k+t+1}=0\}}=1_{\{U_{k,t}\le9\}}$$ are independent Bernoulli variables with success probability $p=9/10$.

Put $N_k=L_k-1$ and $\bar Z_k=N_k^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{N_k}Z_{k,t}$. Under $I_k=1$, each centered variable $Z_{k,t}-p$ has mean zero and second moment $p(1-p)=9/100$; distinct centered variables have zero product expectation by the finite product law of the $U_{k,t}$. Expanding the square and using [F8]–[F9] gives $$\mathbb E[(\bar Z_k-p)^2\mid I_k=1]=\frac{9}{100N_k}.$$ Since $\bar Z_k<4/5$ implies $(\bar Z_k-p)^2>1/100$, Markov's inequality [F10] yields $$\mathbb P(\bar Z_k<4/5\mid I_k=1)\le\frac9{N_k}.$$

Let $H_k=\{I_k=1,\ \bar Z_k\ge4/5\}$. From steps 1.3 and 4.1, $$\mathbb P(H_k)\ge\frac1{k+1}\left(1-\frac9{L_k-1}\right)\ge\frac1{2(k+1)}$$ for all sufficiently large $k$, so $\sum_k\mathbb P(H_k)=\infty$. Each $H_k$ is a function only of coordinate $\Omega_k$, so [F6] makes these events independent. For any fixed $K$, $$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcap_{k=K}^m H_k^c\right)=\prod_{k=K}^m(1-\mathbb P(H_k))\le\exp\!\left(-\sum_{k=K}^m\mathbb P(H_k)\right)\longrightarrow0.$$ Thus the probability of no $H_k$ after $K$ is zero; [F7] applied to the countable union over $K$ shows that infinitely many $H_k$ occur almost surely.

At the endpoint $n_k=s_k+L_k$ of any block with $H_k$, the active outputs $X_{s_k+2},\ldots,X_{s_k+L_k}$ contain at least $(4/5)(L_k-1)$ zeros. Therefore $$\frac1{n_k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}1_{\{X_j=0\}}\ge\frac{(4/5)(L_k-1)}{s_k+L_k}\longrightarrow\frac45$$ along the infinitely many such blocks, by step 1.2. But $\pi(1_{\{0\}})=1/2$. The strong law fails almost surely despite simultaneous uniform ergodicity and diminishing adaptation.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability
kernel on it, meaning that $P(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure for each $x$
and $x\mapsto P(x,A)$ is measurable for each $A\in\mathcal X$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure, that is a countably additive measure of total mass one
([[def-probability-measure]]). The product sigma-algebra
$\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$ is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The joint
flow measure of $(\pi,P)$ is the probability measure $\Lambda_{\pi,P}$ on
$(\mathsf X\times\mathsf X,\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X)$ given, for each
$C\in\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$, by

$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}(C):=\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x:=\{y\in\mathsf X:(x,y)\in C\}.$$

Existence, countable additivity, and the nonnegative iterated-integral identity
for this measure follow from
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. Let $\tau(x,y):=(y,x)$ be
the coordinate-swap map. It is measurable because the preimage of a measurable
rectangle $A\times B$ is $B\times A$ and such rectangles generate the product
sigma-algebra. Define the transpose measure by
$\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}(C):=\Lambda_{\pi,P}(\tau^{-1}(C))$.

The kernel $P$ is **reversible with respect to $\pi$** when
$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}=\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}.$$
This definition uses equality of measures and requires no density, standard
Borel assumption, or prior assumption that $\pi$ is invariant.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a measurable space, $P$ a probability kernel
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) on it, and $\pi$ a probability
measure ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it. If $P$ is reversible with
respect to $\pi$ in the sense of
[[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]], then $\pi$ is
invariant for $P$: for every $A\in\mathcal X$,

$$\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A).$$

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ and $(\Gamma,\mathcal G)$ be nonempty measurable
spaces ([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $\pi$ be a probability measure on
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$, and let $(P_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$ be a jointly
measurable family of probability kernels on $\mathsf X$: for every
$A\in\mathcal X$, $(\gamma,x)\mapsto P_\gamma(x,A)$ is
$\mathcal G\otimes\mathcal X$-measurable and each $P_\gamma$ is a probability
kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]). Assume that $\pi$ is
invariant for every fixed kernel, meaning $\pi P_\gamma=\pi$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]).

An **adaptive MCMC process** is a pair of measurable processes
$(X_n,\Gamma_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $X_n\in\mathsf X$, $\Gamma_n\in\Gamma$, and
natural filtration $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\Gamma_0,\ldots,X_n,\Gamma_n)$,
such that for every $A\in\mathcal X$,
$$\mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=P_{\Gamma_n}(X_n,A)\quad\text{a.s.}$$
The update rule for $\Gamma_{n+1}$ may depend on the history through time
$n+1$; it is required only to make $\Gamma_{n+1}$ a measurable random variable.

For $n\ge0$, define the adaptation size
$$D_n:=\sup_{x\in\mathsf X}\lVert P_{\Gamma_{n+1}}(x,\cdot)-P_{\Gamma_n}(x,\cdot)\rVert_{\rm TV},$$
where total variation uses the convention
$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal X}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]). Assume each $D_n$
is measurable; it lies in $[0,1]$. The process has **diminishing
adaptation** if $D_n\to0$ in probability as $n\to\infty$. This condition does
not require $\Gamma_n$ to converge.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ and $(\Gamma,\mathcal G)$, the jointly
measurable probability-kernel family $(P_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$, common
invariant probability $\pi$, and adaptive process $(X_n,\Gamma_n)$ satisfy
[[def-diminishing-adaptation]]. Fix an initial law $\mu_0$ for
$(X_0,\Gamma_0)$; a fixed initial pair is the Dirac-law special case. If
diminishing adaptation holds under this law and either of the following
conditions holds, then
$$\lVert\mathcal L_{\mu_0}(X_n)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\longrightarrow0.$$

1. **Simultaneous uniform ergodicity:** for every $\epsilon>0$ there is an
   integer $N(\epsilon)\ge1$ such that
   $$\sup_{x\in\mathsf X,\,\gamma\in\Gamma}\lVert P_\gamma^{N(\epsilon)}(x,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\epsilon.$$

2. **Containment:** for every $\epsilon,\delta>0$ there is an integer $N$
   such that
   $$\mathbb P_{\mu_0}\!\left(M_\epsilon(X_n,\Gamma_n)\le N\right)\ge1-\delta\quad\text{for every }n\ge0,$$
   where $M_\epsilon$ is the fixed-kernel convergence time from
   [[def-adaptive-mcmc-containment]].

The conclusion is convergence of the one-time marginal distributions. It does
not itself assert a strong law, a central limit theorem, or convergence of
sample averages.

derivations.claim: The matrix of $P_\gamma$ is $\begin{pmatrix}1-\gamma/2&\gamma/2\\\gamma/2&1-\gamma/2\end{pmatrix}.$ Its rows are probability vectors by $0\le\gamma\le1$ and [F1]. The matrix is symmetric, and $\pi$ assigns equal mass to both states, so the four joint-flow atoms are symmetric under coordinate swap. Thus $P_\gamma$ is reversible by [F2], and $\pi$ is invariant by [F3].
The kernels satisfy $P_{\gamma'}(x,\cdot)-P_\gamma(x,\cdot)=(\gamma'-\gamma)(\pi-\delta_x)$, so $D_n=|\Gamma_{n+1}-\Gamma_n|/2\to0$. This is diminishing adaptation by [F5].

Since $\Pi^2=\Pi$ and $I\Pi=\Pi I=\Pi$, induction gives $P_\gamma^m=(1-\gamma)^mI+\bigl(1-(1-\gamma)^m\bigr)\Pi.$ For either state $x$, $\lVert\delta_x-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}=1/2$, so $\lVert P_\gamma^m(x,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}=(1-\gamma)^m/2\le2^{-m-1}$ uniformly in $x$ and $\gamma\in[1/2,1]$. Therefore the family is simultaneously uniformly ergodic.
Steps 2.1 and 1.2 verify the two hypotheses in alternative 1 of [F6]. Hence $\lVert\mathcal L(X_n)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\to0$ for every initial state.
